title: Rafael and the Will
premise: Wendell Fairweather, the meticulous coroner of Hollow Creek, is hired by a nervous stranger who pays triple rate to prove that Eleanor Voss, the town's wealthiest widow, will be murdered before her new will is signed — a crime that hasn't happened yet. When Wendell digs into the case, he discovers the supposed victim may already be dead, her identity kept alive by a caretaker, and the 'witness' everyone swears is buried in plot forty-one is actually alive and hiding. As Wendell closes in on the truth, he realizes his client orchestrated the whole scheme to force the town to confront an old injustice: Eleanor's fortune was built on a forged will decades ago. In the end, Wendell must choose between the letter of the law and exposing the inheritance fraud, and he does so by letting the living witness testify at last.
about_author: Isandro Voss is the pen name of a former small-town records clerk who spent eleven years filing death certificates and learned that every document hides a second story. They write mysteries about paper trails, quiet towns, and the debts the dead leave behind.

chapters.title: The Client Who Paid for Nothing
chapters.summary: Wendell Fairweather's POV. A pale stranger named Mr. Lark arrives at the coroner's office with an envelope of cash, asking Wendell to prove a murder that hasn't occurred yet — the killing of Eleanor Voss. Wendell, proud of never failing a case, accepts against his better judgment. The beat is uneasy curiosity: a man whose trade is certainty confronting a job built on prediction.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. To establish whether Eleanor Voss is even alive, Wendell walks the cemetery he knows intimately and finds plot forty-one freshly turned but oddly shallow, registered under the name of a witness to the old Voss will. The emotional beat is creeping doubt — the first crack in his confidence that records tell the truth.

chapters.title: The Widow's House
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He visits the Voss estate under pretense of a routine death-record audit and meets the caretaker, Silas Crane, whose answers are too smooth and whose guest wing smells of lye. Wendall glimpses a curtained window move. The beat is dread masked as procedure; the house feels rehearsed, like a stage set between performances.

chapters.title: A Will Signed in Ink and Ash
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Wendell and brief flashbacks from Eleanor's perspective thirty years prior. The chapter reveals the original Voss will was witnessed by three people — one now supposedly in plot forty-one. Wendell begins pulling county archives. The beat is obsession taking root as he realizes the past will is the blueprint for the present crime.

chapters.title: The Witness in Plot Forty-One
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He petitions to examine the grave and finds the coffin empty except for weighted stones and a decades-old coat. Someone has been paying for perpetual care on an empty plot. The beat is vertigo — the town's most reliable record-keeper discovers its most reliable record is a lie.

chapters.title: Lark's Ledger
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Following payment traces, he learns 'Mr. Lark' has hired three investigators before him; two left town abruptly, one vanished. Wendell realizes he may be a pawn in someone's design rather than a detective. The beat is wounded pride curdling into fear as the hunter suspects he is hunted.

chapters.title: Silas Sings a Careful Song
chapters.summary: Dual POV: Wendell interviewing Silas Crane, intercut with Silas's guarded interior monologue. Silas admits Eleanor rarely leaves her room but produces convincing proof of life — a signed check dated last week. Wendell notices the handwriting trembles in a way signatures shouldn't. The beat is a duel of courtesies, each man lying politely.

chapters.title: The Daughter Who Left
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He tracks down Marianne Voss, the estranged daughter, in a neighboring county, who claims she hasn't spoken to her mother in years and stands to inherit nothing under the new will. Her bitterness rings true, but her alibi for the night the witness 'died' is thin. The beat is reluctant sympathy tangled with suspicion.

chapters.title: What the Town Remembers
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV through Wendell's interviews: the pharmacist, the pastor, the retired sheriff. Each recalls the night of the original will signing differently, and each account quietly protects someone. The beat is the theme of memory as inheritance — the town itself keeps a forged version of its own history.

chapters.title: The Vanished Investigator
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He locates the missing predecessor, half-drunk and terrified, hiding in a fishing cabin. The man saw 'Eleanor' alive after her supposed death date and fled. His testimony confirms the timeline is impossible — unless the body in the official record belongs to someone else. The beat is grim validation: Wendell was right, and being right is dangerous.

chapters.title: Midnight at the Mausoleum
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, tense and atmospheric. Watching the Voss mausoleum at night, he sees Silas admit a hooded figure carrying supplies. Wendell follows, loses them in the crypts, and finds fresh food wrappers and medicine bottles — someone is living among the dead. The beat is heart-pounding pursuit ending in revelation by absence.

chapters.title: The Face Behind the Curtain
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Confronting the hidden figure, he discovers not Eleanor but Ruth Calloway — the witness from plot forty-one, alive, aged, and hiding for thirty years because she refused to perjure herself about the original will and was meant to die for it. The beat is awe and grief: the case's central impossibility resolves into a human story of survival.

chapters.title: Who Is Dying, Then?
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV, her first full narration. She explains the plan: someone hired her protectors to stage her survival evidence, but the real target of the coming murder is Eleanor, whose conscience had driven her to rewrite the will honestly. Ruth believes Silas is protecting Eleanor — or imprisoning her. The beat is the mystery pivoting from 'who died' to 'who will die.'

chapters.title: The Check That Trembled
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Forensic comparison shows the recent 'Eleanor' signature was traced by a left-handed forger — Silas is right-handed. Someone else in the house signs for her. Wendell suspects Marianne returned secretly. The beat is cold clarity: the household is a closed loop of impersonation, and time is short.

chapters.title: Mr. Lark Unmasked
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He traps Lark with a fabricated report and forces a confession: Lark is the son of the lawyer who drafted the fraudulent original will, hired by Ruth's allies to force the truth into daylight by manufacturing a crisis no one could ignore. But Lark swears he never intended actual murder — someone has hijacked his scheme. The beat is betrayal inside betrayal.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge: Silas barricades the estate, Marianne arrives unannounced, Ruth insists on going to the house, and Wendell races the weather and the calendar — the new will signs tomorrow. The beat is accelerating dread, chapters tightening like a knot as every player moves toward the same door.

chapters.title: The Room at the End of the Hall
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, breaking into the locked east wing. He finds Eleanor Voss alive but frail, lucid, and complicit: she has been pretending greater decline to test who around her would act on her death. She knows someone means to kill her before the honest will is signed. The beat is quiet devastation — the 'victim' has been investigating her own murder longer than Wendell has.

chapters.title: Confession at the Signing Table
chapters.summary: Climax part one. At the will signing, Wendell stalls proceedings while Ruth enters publicly for the first time in thirty years. Marianne breaks — she discovered the fraud, confronted her mother, and let Silas's protective isolation curdle into control; the 'murder' Lark predicted was her contingency. The beat is cathartic rupture as the town's buried lie surfaces in one room.

chapters.title: Plot Forty-One, Filled
chapters.summary: Climax part two. Silas, cornered, attempts to flee with the fraudulent will's proceeds and is stopped by Wendell and the retired sheriff. In the struggle, the truth of the original forgery — and which parent signed it — comes out fully. The beat is violent resolution: justice outside the law nearly becomes another crime, and Wendell chooses restraint.

chapters.title: What the Law Can't Hold
chapters.summary: Falling action, Wendell's POV. Legal consequences land unevenly: Marianne faces charges, Silas cooperates, Lark disappears again, and much of the old fraud sits beyond any statute of limitations. Wendell wrestles with having proven a murder that both did and didn't happen. The beat is bittersweet reckoning with the limits of paper justice.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Thirty years late, Ruth gives her sworn statement about the original will, and Eleanor executes the honest version with Ruth as witness — the ceremony interrupted three decades ago finally completed. The beat is restoration: memory, given voice, becomes the truest inheritance.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name, Revisited
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, closing mirror of chapter one. He walks the cemetery at dawn, orders a proper stone for plot forty-one bearing Ruth's name while she lives, and files his final report: case closed, no murder committed, one life recovered. A new client waits in his office. The beat is earned peace with an open door — the coroner's faith in records, broken and rebuilt, now includes the living.
